claim: With plain FSDP, the communication of large sparse embedding parameters severely degrades training efficiency and FSDP easily runs out of memory for vocabulary sizes exceeding 5x10^6, so a large n-gram table cannot be trained under a naive data-parallel sharding strategy.
stance_target: The premise that a large frozen-or-trainable n-gram table can be trained under plain DDP/FSDP on 64 GB cards
scope_conditions: OverEncoding embedding tables, FSDP training, vocabulary size m
quoted_support: when parameter sharding strategies, such as FSDP (Zhao et al., 2023), are applied during training, the communication of these sparse parameters can severely degrade training efficiency, further constraining the choice of m (the vocabulary size) to smaller values... without this optimization, FSDP experiences a 25% slowdown and easily runs out of memory for vocabulary sizes exceeding m = 5 x 10^6.

claim: The recommended fix for large embedding tables is tensor parallelism scoped to the embedding layer: row-wise shard the table across all data-parallel ranks, send each token to the rank holding its row, and send the vector back - two all-to-all in the forward pass and one all-to-all in the backward pass, with total communication volume significantly lower than FSDP.
stance_target: Whether training a large memory table requires a collective-capable fabric rather than plain DDP
quoted_support: We recommend using tensor parallelism specifically for the over-encoding embedding layer to reduce communication overhead. The embedding table is row-wise sharded across all data-parallel (DP) ranks... This process involves two all-to-all communications during the forward pass and one all-to-all communication during the backward pass, resulting in a total communication volume significantly lower than that of FSDP.

claim: With the embedding-parallel optimization, training an over-encoded model at vocabulary size m = 10^7 on FSDP loses less than 5% throughput.
stance_target: The magnitude of training-throughput cost from a very large memory table
scope_conditions: OverEncoding with m = 10^7, FSDP plus embedding-layer tensor parallelism
quoted_support: We implement this optimization and find that training an over-encoded model with m = 10^7 on FSDP reduces throughput by less than 5%.

claim: The paper proposes, but does not measure, a dedicated embedding-lookup pipeline stage that overlaps embedding communication with the transformer forward of the current micro-batch and would allow over-encoding parameters to be offloaded to CPU, completely alleviating GPU memory pressure.
stance_target: Whether CPU offload of memory tables during training is demonstrated or merely proposed
scope_conditions: Section 3.3 proposed design, citing Fang et al. 2022 and Li et al. 2023
quoted_support: we can design a dedicated embedding lookup stage in a pipeline-parallel training framework, which overlaps the communication required for embedding lookups with the transformer forward of the current micro-batch... Additionally, under this approach, the over-encoding parameters could be offloaded to the CPU, completely alleviating GPU memory pressure.

claim: Input vocabulary size has a log-linear relationship with training loss: OE-12.8M matches a baseline 2.5x larger in model scale at no additional training cost.
stance_target: Whether scaling memory capacity is a cheaper axis than scaling model parameters
scope_conditions: OLMo2-151M/400M/1B, 400B tokens for 151M and 400M, 1T tokens for 1B
quoted_support: the OE-12.8M model achieves comparable performance to a baseline model that is 2.5 times larger in model scale (comparing the 400M OE model with the 1B baseline model)... This observation suggests a log-linear relationship between vocabulary size and model performance.

claim: OverEncoding accelerates convergence substantially: a 5.7x training-loss speedup on OLMo2-1B at 1T tokens, with downstream accelerations of 3.2x, 3.0x and 2.6x on MMLU-Var, HellaSwag and ARC respectively.
stance_target: The compute-efficiency payoff of memory scaling
quoted_support: From the perspective of convergence acceleration, training loss achieves a remarkable 5.7x speedup... OE exhibits substantial acceleration, achieving 3.2x, 3.0x, 2.6x.

claim: OverEncoding on MoE backbones adds 12.8M input-vocabulary parameters and yields only modest downstream gains: OLMoE-1.3B goes 1.3B -> 13.1B params with loss -0.082 and downstream +0.014, while OLMoE-7B goes 7B -> 26.3B with loss -0.076 and downstream +0.007.
stance_target: Whether n-gram memory scaling delivers on sparse MoE backbones
scope_conditions: OLMoE-1.3B (260M active) and OLMoE-7B (1.3B active), 500B tokens, base vocab 50280

claim: Engram's own comparison states that OverEncoding fails to yield meaningful improvements on sparse MoE backbones even under a non-isoparametric setting, which is consistent with the small MoE deltas OverEncoding reports.
stance_target: Cross-source agreement that naive n-gram averaging underperforms on MoE
scope_conditions: Engram related-work section, citing Huang et al. 2025a
quoted_support: Similarly, OverEncoding (Huang et al., 2025a) fails to yield meaningful improvements on sparse MoE backbones even under a non-isoparametric setting.
